mcqs.question: A codebase enforces permissions with scattered `if user.id == 4521` checks across dozens of files. What's the main structural problem authorization models solve that this approach doesn't?
options: It runs slower than a centralized permission check at runtime
It's fundamentally impossible to express any permission logic this way
It can't be audited or centrally updated — answering 'who can delete invoices' requires reading every conditional in the codebase, and changing policy requires a code deploy
It only works for a single user, never multiple users
mcqs.explanation: Scattered hardcoded checks encode business policy as buried application logic — there's no single place to inspect or change 'who can do what,' and every policy change needs a deploy rather than a data update. It's not necessarily slower at runtime, it can technically express logic for multiple users, and the problem is auditability and maintainability, not fundamental expressiveness.

mcqs.question: In RBAC, why does adding a new permission to the `editor` role automatically apply to every user assigned that role, with no per-user updates?
options: Because RBAC re-authenticates every user whenever a role changes
Because roles are only usable by exactly one user at a time
Because RBAC systems automatically re-run a database migration on every permission change
Because users are assigned to roles, not directly to permissions, so updating the role definition updates what every assigned user can do through that indirection
mcqs.explanation: The indirection layer — users connect to roles, roles connect to permissions — means the role definition is the single source of truth, so editing it once propagates to every user holding that role. No re-authentication or migration step is involved, and roles are explicitly meant to be shared across many users, not scoped to one.

mcqs.question: A policy needs to allow document access only during business hours and only for documents matching the user's department. Why is ABAC a better fit for this than RBAC?
options: ABAC evaluates a rule against attributes like time and department directly, while RBAC would need a combinatorial explosion of roles to express the same conditions
RBAC cannot express any conditional logic under any circumstances
ABAC is always faster to evaluate than a role lookup
RBAC roles automatically expire outside business hours by default
mcqs.explanation: ABAC expresses time- and department-dependent access as one rule referencing attributes, whereas RBAC would need a distinct role for every combination of department and time window it wants to support, quickly multiplying roles. RBAC can express some conditions through role structure, just clumsily here; ABAC isn't inherently faster, and RBAC roles don't auto-expire based on time of day.

mcqs.question: Two documents owned by the same user need completely different, unrelated sharing lists. Which authorization model naturally fits this requirement?
options: RBAC, since roles can be customized per document
None of these models can express per-document sharing differences
ABAC, since attributes are always tied to the owning user
ACLs, since each resource carries its own independent list of who can access it
mcqs.explanation: ACLs attach permissions to the resource itself, so two documents can have entirely independent sharing lists with no relationship to each other — exactly this scenario. RBAC roles apply broadly rather than per-resource-instance, ABAC attributes aren't inherently tied to the owner, and this is precisely the case ACLs are designed to handle.

mcqs.question: A team keeps creating near-duplicate roles like `editor-us` and `editor-eu` that differ only by region. What does this signal, and what's the fix?
options: Nothing is wrong; this is the intended way to scale RBAC
The system needs more roles, not fewer — region should get its own dedicated role hierarchy
This signals role explosion, and the region condition should move into an ABAC-style attribute rule instead of a family of near-duplicate roles
This means RBAC is fundamentally incompatible with the system and must be replaced by ACLs
mcqs.explanation: Creating a new role because of a condition rather than a genuinely distinct set of responsibilities is the concrete signature of role explosion, and the fix is expressing that condition as an attribute check rather than multiplying roles. It isn't the intended scaling pattern, more roles would make the problem worse, and ACLs solve a different problem (per-resource sharing), not per-condition role variation.

mcqs.question: Why does role explosion specifically undermine RBAC's main advantage over hardcoded permission checks?
options: Because it makes the system authenticate users more slowly

Because dozens of near-identical roles reintroduce the same audit and maintenance burden RBAC's role indirection was meant to eliminate — you're back to reading many similar definitions to find the real difference
Because RBAC roles cannot be created dynamically at runtime
Because role explosion only affects systems using ABAC, not RBAC
mcqs.explanation: RBAC's value was turning 'who can do X' into a single role lookup; once roles multiply into near-duplicates differing by a condition, answering that same question again requires comparing many similar definitions, which is the exact maintenance burden the model was supposed to remove. This isn't an authentication-speed issue, roles absolutely can be created dynamically, and role explosion is specifically an RBAC failure mode, not an ABAC one.
